cards.front: Recall a key point about Monetary Policy
cards.back: Monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply to influence the economy, primarily to control inflation (Bank of England's 2% CPI target).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Monetary Policy
cards.back: Raising interest rates: reduces borrowing and spending, cools demand, lowers inflation, but may reduce growth and increase unemployment.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Monetary Policy
cards.back: Lowering interest rates: stimulates borrowing and spending, boosts growth, but may cause inflation if demand exceeds supply.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Monetary Policy
cards.back: The Bank of England's MPC sets the base rate monthly, independently from government. Independence prevents politicians setting rates for electoral gain.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Monetary Policy
cards.back: Limitations: time lags (rate changes take 12-18 months to fully affect the economy), can't address supply-side problems, and zero lower bound.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating monetary policy, use the RIT framework: Rapidity (how fast does it take effect?), Impact (how large is the effect?), Targeting (can it address the specific problem?).
Interest rates, QE (e.g. Government spending, taxation)
Relatively quick (days) (e.g. Slow (months for Budget, longer to implement))
Affects whole economy broadly (e.g. Can target specific sectors/groups)
Bank Rate cut to 0.1% in 2020 (e.g. Furlough scheme costing 68 billion pounds)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Monetary policy is always more effective than fiscal policy because it can be changed quickly. Correct: While monetary policy changes quickly, its effects take 12-18 months to transmit through the economy. It's also less effective when interest rates are near zero, the problem is supply-side, or banks refuse to lend (credit crunch). Neither policy is unive
